svg.aria-label: Two maps of the Arabian Peninsula, before the war and now. Before: one thick gold ribbon of about seventeen million barrels a day leaves the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz. Now: that ribbon is a thread of about two million barrels a day; a blue ribbon of five million barrels a day runs west across Saudi Arabia along the East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea, with a red burst marking where it was hit on 10 September; a thin green ribbon leaves Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman.
svg.text: How Gulf crude gets out — before the war, and now
million barrels a day; ribbon width is proportional to flow
≈17 mb/d out, nearly all through Hormuz;
≈9 mb/d out: Hormuz ≈2 · Yanbu 5 (pipe cap. 7) · Fujairah ≈1.5
— and the blue line is now shut
Flows: Kpler via Al Jazeera (Gulf crude exports 17→9 mb/d, Aug 2026); East–West pipeline 7 mb/d capacity, ≈5 mb/d in use (OilPrice, CNBC);
Habshan–Fujairah line ≈1.5 mb/d (CNBC). Same scale in both panels; the pre-war Yanbu and Fujairah flows are drawn thin, unnumbered —
their pre-war throughput is not in the sources. Coastlines: Natural Earth (public domain).
